changes.before: The surviving sibling adaptor slot (`routing_adaptor`) sits in front of a **fixed internal contract** in the gateway — the six-verdict vocabulary the pipeline branches on — and the `spec` / `review` / `ship` contracts are producer-emitted (the producer self-declares a `faff-contract:<name>` block the consumer parses; their adaptor slots were retired). Rendering has none of that: no pipeline code branches on, counts, or gates on how output *looks*. It is purely human-facing. changes.after: `routing_adaptor` translates into the gateway's fixed six-verdict contract. changes.before: Unlike `spec` — which is produced by `faffter-noon-spec` (issue → new spec, self-declaring its `faff-contract:spec-readiness` block the consumer parses) — rendering has no separable generative act. There's no "render from nothing": every render is a transform of data some other skill already holds, and choosing the right form (cycle bracket vs cycle box) needs the domain understanding of what that structure *means*. So a standalone rendering *producer* would have no natural caller. What rendering genuinely is, is a standard **referenced by many skills** (every sub-skill renders "according to" it) plus a standalone normalise act — exactly the adaptor shape. The "produce" the producer-framing reaches for is already the validate/normalise face below. Don't re-split this into a `faffter-noon-rendering`.
changes.after: `faffter-noon-spec` produces a spec from an issue and self-declares `faff-contract:spec-readiness`. Rendering instead transforms data another skill holds; choosing forms (cycle bracket vs cycle box) requires understanding that structure. It has no separable generative act or natural standalone producer caller. Its shared standard plus invokable normalise pass is the adaptor; do not split out `faffter-noon-rendering`.

changes.before: Everything this adaptor defines and normalises applies to **all human-facing output a faff sub-skill emits: terminal output, tracker descriptions, and tracker comments alike** (gateway → **Rendering**, Universal-routing rule). changes.after: Apply all rules to **all human-facing faff output: terminal output, tracker descriptions and tracker comments** (gateway → **Rendering**, Universal-routing rule). Only skill source files (`skills/*/SKILL.md`) and internal `.faff/` logs are exempt. With no central emit point, each skill runs normalisation immediately before printing or writing.

changes.start: Form is half of house style
changes.before: Form is half of house style; the other half is the **voice** the prose reads in — casual-but-credible, claims discipline, the banned-word list. Those rules have a single home: the **`# Writing style`** section of **`AGENTS.md`** at the repo root, a fixed repo convention. This section *references* that section and never copies it — the rules live there so they have one place to drift from, not two (and the `faff validate-adapters` dedup lint fails CI on any block copied across skills).
changes.after: Voice (casual-but-credible, claims discipline, banned words) lives only in repo-root **`AGENTS.md`**, **`# Writing style`**. Reference it; never copy it. This fixed convention keeps one source; `faff validate-adapters` fails CI on blocks duplicated across skills.
preserved_obligations: fixed AGENTS Writing style single source

changes.before: **Injection.** Voice reaches a context-stripped executor the same way form reaches the reader: through the dispatch envelope. The gateway stamps a one-line pointer at the STYLE source into every dispatch that writes durable prose — the mechanism, its carrier rule, and the engine-lane fork all live at gateway → **Producer dispatch → Voice clause**. This charter owns *what* the house voice is for; the gateway owns *how* it rides each dispatch.
changes.after: **Injection.** Every durable-prose dispatch carries a one-line STYLE-source pointer for context-stripped executors. The gateway owns the envelope, carrier rule and engine-lane fork (gateway → **Producer dispatch → Voice clause**); this charter owns voice's purpose.

changes.before: **Swapping the voice.** A project with a different voice edits the `# Writing style` section of `AGENTS.md` — same path, different contents, read fresh on the next dispatch (nothing caches it). The source path is a fixed convention, not adaptor-resolved: dispatch sites stamp the pointer without reading this adaptor first. Swapping the *adaptor* changes form rules and validation; it does not change where the voice rules live.
changes.after: **Swapping the voice.** Edit `AGENTS.md`'s `# Writing style`; each dispatch reads it fresh, without caching. Dispatch sites stamp this fixed pointer without reading the adaptor. Swapping the adaptor changes form and validation, not the voice source path.

changes.before: **Fold, not a sibling.** Voice is folded into this adaptor rather than split into a sibling `voice` slot. Voice and form are both purely human-facing with no pipeline contract behind them — the exact property that defines this slot — so they belong in the one skill that already owns "how faff's output reads", with one swap point instead of two. The charter widening to name voice is deliberate, recorded here. A sibling `voice` adaptor stays a clean future extraction if a project ever needs voice swappable independently of form.
changes.after: **Fold, not a sibling.** Voice and form share this human-facing, contract-free adaptor and one swap point. Do not split a sibling `voice` slot now; independent voice swapping remains a possible future extraction.

changes.start: The gloss is a delivery lead briefing
changes.before: The gloss is a delivery lead briefing a colleague, not a project manager filing a status report. A delivery lead bridges product, engineering, and business stakeholders by making work understandable, bite-sized, and transparent. Leaning on numbered references to internal documents — "principle 6", "ADR-N", "trigger 4", "PRs 3-N" — is the opposite: project-management smoke-and-mirrors that makes the writer look indispensable while making the reader work to decode it.
changes.after: Write the gloss as a delivery lead briefing a colleague: make work understandable, bite-sized and transparent across product, engineering and business. Internal document references such as "principle 6", "ADR-N", "trigger 4", "PRs 3-N" make the reader decode the report instead.

changes.before: **Surface the concrete** (the positive twin of the ban above). Where the source provides a real, checkable noun — the actual field name (`cache_read_input_tokens`), the named file, the specific subsystem — render that, not a category label that abstracts it away. The ban says "don't hide behind principle 6"; this says "name the real thing the source already holds."
changes.after: **Surface the concrete** (the positive twin of the ban). When the source provides a checkable noun, render it instead of an abstract category: the actual field (`cache_read_input_tokens`), named file or specific subsystem. Name what the source holds, not "principle 6".

changes.before: **Why this matters:** faff is a delivery lead, not a project manager. A delivery lead humanises work; a project manager codifies it to look valuable. We do the first. Every finding, every brief, every diagnosis renders the *substance* of what's going on, not the index entry that catalogues it.
changes.after: **Why this matters:** every finding, brief and diagnosis must render the substance, not the document's index entry. Humanise work rather than codifying it to look valuable.

changes.start: Markdown tables break in narrow terminals
changes.before: Markdown tables break in narrow terminals when cells are long. They render as `Column 1: …` repeated per row, mid-word truncation, and rows crashing into each other — the data is technically present but unreadable.
changes.after: Long-cell markdown tables break in narrow terminals: repeated `Column 1: …`, mid-word truncation and colliding rows make data unreadable.

It does **not** apply to skill source files (`skills/*/SKILL.md`) — those are documentation read in wider contexts (Claude Code editor panes, GitHub UI), where specification tables with prose cells are fine. It also does not apply to internal `.faff/runs/<run-id>/…` logs.
changes.after: **Scope:** all human-facing terminal output (diagnostics, morning briefs, roadmap renders, in-conversation summaries), tracker descriptions and comments, per **Scope — all human-facing faff output**. Exempt: skill sources (`skills/*/SKILL.md`), where prose-cell specification tables are fine in wider editor/GitHub views, and internal `.faff/runs/<run-id>/…` logs.
